newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. rates dominate Asian fund flows - experts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rates dominate Asian fund flows - experts.

text.p: United States interest rates are dominating investment flows around Asia, prompting a wave of cash into Hong Kong on bullishness about the territory's business prospects through 1997, experts said on Wednesday.

"Most people are already overweight Hong Kong, and that reflects the fact that U.S. rates have not gone up and the (U.S.) long bond yield is coming down," said Christopher Day, joint managing director at Thornton Management (Asia) Ltd.
Day said Hong Kong's currency peg to the U.S. dollar allows the British colony to benefit from cheaper overnight money and a falling long-bond yield in the United States, now at 6.81 percent.

Hong Kong is also gaining as American institutional investors unwind cash positions built up in anticipation of a U.S. rate hike, said Marshall Mays, regional strategist at Nikko Research Centre (Hong Kong) Ltd.

"The fact the Fed didn't raise interest rates a couple of weeks ago has caused people to take their cash and put it somewhere. They put it into Hong Kong because it is the cheapest to execute in Asia. If money is cheap, cash is not interesting any more," Mays said.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng index soared nearly 228 points to 12,133.07 on Monday before shedding 26.31 points to 12,106.76 on Tuesday. The index resumed its upward path on Wednesday, gaining almost 85 points to 12,191.67 late in the trading day.
Experts said confidence in Hong Kong was increasing.
A more conciliatory tone from China had diminished international nervousness associated with the colony's return next year to Chinese rule, they said.
At the same time a strong property sector, falling inflation, hints of improved consumer confidence and steady growth rates all suggested Hong Kong's economy was poised for a turnaround, they said.

"It's already experiencing something of a turnaround from a low base and that makes financial assets more attractive," said Day. "Equally, you might find the larger institutions have already thought this through and are already here."
Day believes expectations of corporate earnings performance through 1997 will determine longer-term direction.
"For the market to really run, you need to see earnings growth expectations improve and it's probably a bit too early for that," he said.

Mays believes the U.S. bond yield curve, which he expects to steepen, will also be a factor for the Hong Kong market, as will a resumption of interest rate uncertainty following the U.S. election in November.
"I think this (cash unwinding) is short-lived," he said.
Most flows into Hong Kong are believed to be coming from the United States and Japan, contrary to some reports that international funds were reallocating assets within the region.
Strategists said they reallocated Hong Kong some weeks ago, adding that local factors were the primary drivers of weakness in countries like Thailand and the Philippines.
Thailand continues to suffer from a combination of bad economic and political news, while the Philippines has succumbed to profit-taking, they said.

"The Philippines has had a good run and now there's an element of profit-taking," Day said. "But I wouldn't avoid the Philippines because some of the new companies coming to the market and some of the high growth companies listed over the last 12 months still look attractive."
Mays added: "Foreigners have been the main sellers in the Philippines, but the liquidity is still there...I think Manila will be back up to 32 or 33 by the end of the year."
